items.title: Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
items.summary: Indonesian authorities say another 13 are missing in the illegal gold mine, which flooded on Monday.
items.body:
Image source, Basarnas, National Search and Rescue Agency

Image caption,

The flooded mine is in Bogor in West Java

ByGavin Butler, BBC Indonesia and Aditya Nugraha, Reporting fromin Pongkor

It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.

Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.

Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.

Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.

Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.

"We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday.

"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."

Image source, Basarnas, National Search and Rescue Agency

Image caption,

Rescuers have been working day and night to find survivors in the flooded mine shaft

Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.

Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high – spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.

This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.

On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.

But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.

"[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.

"It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."

Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.

Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".

"As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.

In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.

Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.

But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common – whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Relatives of the missing Bogor miners have been waiting near the site for news of their loved ones

Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.

Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.

There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.

Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear".

"Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."

The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it.

"This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.

"We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.

"Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."

As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.

More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.

As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

items.title: DR Congo demands answers over Ugandan general's threats
items.summary: Gen Kainerugaba threatened a rebel takeover of a mineral-rich area in DR Congo in controversial X posts.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba's social media posts have previously sparked diplomatic tensions

ByWycliffe Muia

Updated 1 hour ago

The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.

In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.

The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.

The Ugandan government has yet to respond.

The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.

Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.

Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.

• Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession feverPublished14 November

• The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on TwitterPublished30 October 2022

In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.

The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.

They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.

He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.

Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.

Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.

It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.

During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."

The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.

Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.

"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.

"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".

The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".

It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.

In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.

In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.

The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.

In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

items.title: How Chinese companies circumvent chips sanctions in Southeast Asia
items.summary: High-tech AI chips are hard to get in China because of US restrictions. To get around this, Chinese companies often use offshore computing capacity, particularly in Southeast Asia. The US is also trying to stop it.
items.body:

Dozens of data centers have been built in Malaysia in recent yearsImage: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/picture alliance

Advertisement

Some €510 billion ($559 billion) have been invested into AI infrastructure across Malaysia since February 2025. The consulting group Fitch Solutions has opened 125 data centers in Malaysia to serve the global digital economy. The sector is booming in the western Malaysian state of Johor where, according to Malaysia's Digital Ministry, 16 of 27 new data centers are located.

The government in Kuala Lumpur hopes the investment will create numerous new jobs, up to 90% of which are expected to be filled by locals. The advantages of the data center sites include low electricity prices for energy-intensive computing and good links to international submarine cables.

Amazon, Google and Microsoft along Strait of Malacca

Major US technology companies have also set up along the Strait of Malacca. Amazon and Oracle have each invested $6 billion, while Microsoft and Google have invested $2 billion apiece. In early November, Google's parent company, Alphabet, announced additional investments of $15 billion.

"Malaysia's vision is not only to build an economy that uses artificial intelligence, but also one that uses AI creatively,” explained Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo in a statement that was tellingly published in Chinese, which is not an official language of Malaysia.

Trump's ASEAN Play: The new front in the US-China chip war

Data center growth in Southeast Asia is part of the race for technological supremacy in artificial intelligence. The US has restricted the export of high-performance chips, such as those produced by US tech giant Nvidia, to China. It has also tried to block the sale of the advanced lithography machines used to manufacture microchips that are made by Dutch manufacturer ASML.

Chinese companies rent access to US chips

Since Chinese chips have yet to reach the same technological standards as others, some Chinese companies are testing an alternative model in that they legally purchase or lease capacity in other countries. They can thus rent access to US chips that have been installed in systems in Malaysia, for example, and develop their AI models from abroad.

In October, the Institute for Progress (IFP), an independent think tank in Washington, warned that Southeast Asia was becoming an offshore hub for Chinese AI enclaves. It estimated that by the end of the year about 24% of China's total computing power came from remote access to overseas data centers, three-quarters of which were in Southeast Asia. This was predicted to rise to 31% by the end of 2027.

Most of the workers at the data centers in Malaysia are locals Image: Cheng Yiheng/Xinhua/picture alliance

The IFP said that though "US AI chips hosted in overseas data centers are a significant source of compute for China," they were "difficult to size."

It explained that "Chinese entities can rent GPUs [graphics processing units] as a service from cloud providers or lease data center capacity overseas, directly from developers or through intermediaries. Cloud providers and data center developers rarely name their customers or disclose how much capacity each uses, and Chinese companies disclose little themselves."

Alibaba Cloud sets up shop in Malaysia

The Chinese giant Alibaba Cloud currently operates six data centers in Malaysia — three in Johor and three in the greater Kuala Lumpur region, with the most recent one opening on November 19.

The company has invested $53 billion in data centers in total, including in South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines and Mexico, as well as Malaysia. TikTok's parent company also operates data center capacity in Johor.

The race for transformers

In early October, Tencent, another multinational technology conglomerate, which is based in Shenzhen, signed a five-year $7 billion contract with Oracle, allowing it to use computing capacity equivalent to 100,000 modern AI chips for training artificial intelligence. The company was supposed to pay 30% upfront.

The deal fell through a few weeks later, however, and both companies have remained silent about the reasons. According to media reports, there was pressure from the governments in both Beijing and Washington. China wants to develop its own chip industry, whereas high-ranking US officials reportedly raised security concerns with Oracle.

US tariffs on Malaysian imports

In mid-2025, the US threatened to impose an additional 25% tariff on Malaysia imports "to prevent circumvention of export controls on chips," according to the Chinese consulting firm Equal Ocean. "The Malaysian government quickly responded by opposing illegal resale practices and introducing licensing requirements for the transshipment of certain high-end chips."

Washington is now stepping up its efforts. On the same day that US President Donald Trump met with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China last week, the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency of the US Department of Commerce, issued new rules with regard to remote access to advanced AI chips and servers.

It said that the goal was "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests." The restrictions pertain to data centers that provide significant computing capacity to companies with ties to countries in "Country Group D:5 or Macau."

How the China-US AI arms race is escalating

According to US export regulations, the D:5 group includes China, Russia, Iran and North Korea and others. In future, companies will have to conduct more thorough checks to identify the ownership and control structures behind their clients.

Washington has also introduced new licensing requirements for advanced semiconductors destined for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Subsidiaries of US companies are exempt.

"The US is not only reviewing which countries will receive AI chips in future but also wants to have a say in where the chips are used, who operates them and which customers they serve," explained Chinese industry expert Xu Sanlang. "This means that data centers, which have been providing remote computing capacity to Chinese clients will have to comply with these restrictions in future."

This article was originally written in German.

Nvidia has told its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers to four Southeast Asian countries, as the US steps up export controls to prevent Chinese access to AI computing power.

Manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro, which package Nvidia’s chips into servers, have told buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that Nvidia will not allow their orders to be shipped, according to three people with knowledge of the matter.

It is unclear whether the halt is temporary, as Nvidia and its partners try to work out how to comply with Washington’s new export controls, the people said.

The four Southeast Asian countries have become favoured destinations for Chinese AI developers seeking to access Nvidia’s most advanced chips, whose exports are restricted by Washington.

items.title: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
items.summary: Female protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, a rights group says.
items.body:
Image source, Supplied by family

Image caption,

Twin sisters Romina (left) and Taraneh Rahimi were arrested in late January, their cousin says

ByBy Soroush Pakzad

BBC News Persian

Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.

In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.

She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.

He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.

He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.

Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.

Image source, Anonymous/Getty Images

Image caption,

January's protests began over economic grievances and spread to become Iran's largest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution

The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".

The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

Image source, Instagram

Image caption,

Taraneh loves horses and would like to set up her own breeding centre one day, her cousin says

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.

Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".

Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.

Image source, Supplied to human rights groups

Image caption,

This image of Mahboubeh Shabani, sentenced to death in September, has been shared with human rights groups

Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.

Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.

"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.

The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.

The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."

Image source, Supplied to Hrana

Image caption,

Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, rights groups say

Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".

At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".

Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".

Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".

In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".

Image source, Supplied by family

Image caption,

Taraneh (left) and Romina both say they gave baseless confessions after being tortured

Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.

Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."

Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.

Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.

Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.

Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.

Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

items.title: Can Rassvet, 'Russia's Starlink' change the course of the war in Ukraine?
items.summary: SpaceX's US Starlink satellite system has played a key role in countering the Russian military in Ukraine, but now a Russian counterpart is under development. What could this mean for Ukraine?
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PtKd

Prefer DW on Google

Electronic warfare is an important component in Russia's war against Ukraine Image: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance

Advertisement

Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX. Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit. Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine. On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.

Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.

In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.

In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.

Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's dependence on satellites

What is Rassvet?

Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026. According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks. The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.

HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory."

Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027.

According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president, the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory. He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there.

Starlink terminals are used by both the Russian and Ukrainian armies for communications Image: Lev Radin/picture alliance

SpaceX remains far superior to Rassvet in tech terms

Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept."

"When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.

He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company. He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components."

"Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin said. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being."

SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors. According to DW's sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not currently require as many satellites as Starlink. Ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes.

But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos. In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled.

Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?

Did SpaceX throttle Starlink in Ukraine?

Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine. "Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher.

Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23.

When asked by DW whether the Ukrainian military could gain access to Rassvet, Trishkin said it was "only a matter of time" before terminals fell "into foreign hands and are subsequently examined."

Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX. Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit. Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine. On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.

Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.

In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.

In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.
Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's dependence on satellites
What is Rassvet?

Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026. According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks. The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.
HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory."

Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027.

According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president, the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory. He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there.
Starlink terminals are used by both the Russian and Ukrainian armies for communications Image: Lev Radin/picture alliance
SpaceX remains far superior to Rassvet in tech terms

Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept."

"When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.

He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company. He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components."

"Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin said. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being."

SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors. According to DW's sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not currently require as many satellites as Starlink. Ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes.

But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos. In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Did SpaceX throttle Starlink in Ukraine?

Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine. "Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher.
Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23.
When asked by DW whether the Ukrainian military could gain access to Rassvet, Trishkin said it was "only a matter of time" before terminals fell "into foreign hands and are subsequently examined."

S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch

S&P said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects.

File photo. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks with Alice Huang after delivering a keynote speech at COMPUTEX 2024 in Taipei, Taiwan, Jun 2, 2024. (Photo: Reuters/Ann Wang)

S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade on Wednesday (Nov 25), saying the departure and subsequent reinstatement of its CEO had exposed weaknesses in the chipmaker's management and board oversight.

"We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence. The company's corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler," the ratings agency said.

The move comes amid a turbulent period for Nvidia's leadership. The company's board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang earlier this week, days after he resigned following revelations of extramarital affairs with his direct reports as well as a Chinese businesswoman alleged by US intelligence to be Beijing's spy.

Critics and lawmakers slammed the reinstatement, questioning the independence of the board, whose newly elected chair had told investors last week Nvidia would not rehire Huang as CEO because his personal behaviour was inconsistent with the company's code of conduct.

Reinstating Huang on Monday, Nvidia omitted any mention of his affairs, saying instead the move was "based on US government input", even as an independent board committee continued its investigation into reports involving him and a suspected foreign intelligence effort.

Reuters reported on Wednesday that the US Justice Department did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before US President Donald Trump pushed for his return as CEO, according to three people familiar with the matter.

Instead, it concluded that there was no evidence he had broken any laws based on ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China. That determination is subject to change as the probes continue.

Jensen Huang’s stunning return as Nvidia CEO: A timeline of events

Inside the ‘war room’ that lobbied Donald Trump to bring back Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

NO EVIDENCE YET THAT ALICE HUANG IS A SPY

Investors were largely unruffled by the S&P move, which comes with Nvidia shares down 38 per cent since Oct 6. Nvidia closed down nearly 4 per cent on Wednesday, retracing some declines after the Nasdaq 100 index briefly flirted with a 20 per cent decline from its recent high.

The cost of insurance against tech companies defaulting on debts has jumped sharply in recent weeks, but the five-year CDS spread for Nvidia was little changed.

Nvidia currently has an AA rating from S&P, which indicates a very strong capacity to meet financial commitments. The highest rating is AAA.

The agency said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects.

Meanwhile, Moody's said on Wednesday that bringing back Huang eases near-term uncertainty around Nvidia's business execution and eliminates execution risk associated with appointing a new leader for the chipmaker.

The agency said Nvidia's Aa1 rating and stable outlook remain unaffected, but added that governance and regulatory uncertainty persists.

Nvidia has played a key role in financing the AI boom, bankrolling AI startups, cloud firms and data-center projects, which in turn spend much of that capital on Nvidia's own GPUs and other AI chips.

The complex financing arrangements have increased Nvidia's exposure to a potential downturn, analysts said.

Separately, the Wall Street Journal on Wednesday reported that US officials found no evidence that tech executive Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on Jensen Huang, citing people familiar with a classified briefing.

Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director of National Intelligence and National Security Agency briefed staff from congressional intelligence committees and chamber leaders, the Journal reported.

The officials said Alice Huang contacted China's spy agency during the affair but found no indication that she provided significant intelligence, the Journal reported.

Nvidia and the agencies did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report.

The report said current evidence suggests Alice Huang and Jensen Huang may have had an amorous relationship, but it was not a coordinated play by China, and that new information could change that assessment.

The briefing also noted that Kang Wei, described to the Journal as Alice Huang's husband by people who know them, was an asset for China's Ministry of State Security who remained in frequent contact with the intelligence service.

Source: Reuters/aj

items.body:
Figure caption,

Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter

ByJessica Parker, Berlin correspondent and Tom Beal, BBC News Investigations

A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.

Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled)

At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.

There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.

In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."

It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.

French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.

The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.

While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".

Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.

In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.

In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.

Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.

News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.

He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

Image caption,

One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cans

The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.

Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.

The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.

"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

• Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.

Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.

Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.

On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.

The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

Image caption,

Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police

Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.

Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.

The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.

Image caption,

We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules

When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.

He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.

It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

Image caption,

Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.

The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.

Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.

The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police
Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.
Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.
The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.

blocks.alt: Blurred face of a man who has brown hair and a beard. He is holding a phone to his right ear. There is a metal fence to his right and trees behind him.

blocks.text: Image caption,
We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules
When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.
He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.
It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

blocks.text: Image caption,
Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.
The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.
Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.
The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every American child

The silhouette of Elon Musk, SpaceX logo and a rising stock graph are seen in this illustration taken on Jun 11, 2026. (Image: Reuters/Dado Ruvic)

Elon Musk, the world's richest person, said on Wednesday (Nov 25) that every child in the US will receive two shares in SpaceX, the space and AI company he runs, pledging a gift worth some US$18 billion.

Musk and rival AI company Anthropic have recently laid out sharply different blueprints for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom, amid growing public and political scrutiny of the industry.

Children will receive one share from the company and one from him personally, Musk said in a brief post on X, without providing details.

In a separate post, Musk said the SpaceX shares will be transferred next month.

"The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," Musk added.

SpaceX said earlier on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, adding that Musk will personally match the number of shares donated by the company.

A Trump Account is a program designed to give Americans under the age of 18 a stake in the stock market and help build wealth from an early age. The White House said in October it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at US$127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly US$18 billion.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Musk's SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts.

"What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base," said Christopher Brankin, global markets advisor at brokerage Mitrade Group. "It builds immediate market engagement and creates a massive, financially literate client pipeline for trading platforms as that generation comes of age."

Musk, whose net worth is around US$824 billion, said last month he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June.

"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X at the time.

"Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way," Musk added.

Most of Musk's philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than US$14 billion in assets.

In October, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under the Trump initiative.

Anthropic, which recently went public, said last month it was committing 5 per cent of its shares to a new fund for the "public good".

It said that the initiative, worth around US$54 billion at current prices, will give it more flexibility and scale to make donations for the benefit of humanity.

Other executives have also set up major, long-running philanthropy ventures.

Berkshire Hathaway Chairman Emeritus Warren Buffett, one of the most prominent figures in philanthropy, is reported to have given away US$60 billion so far, with most of the rest of his roughly US$150 billion fortune slated for philanthropy too.

The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has distributed more than US$100 billion since its founding in 2000, with some of that fueled by donations from Buffett.

items.summary: This strategy of forcing trading partners to the negotiating table may not work as it once did, says Steven Okun from APAC Advisors.

Commentary

Commentary: New US tariff threat seeks to ramp up pressure on trading partners – will it work?

This strategy of forcing trading partners to the negotiating table may not work as it once did, says Steven Okun from APAC Advisors.

A 3D-printed miniature model depicting U.S. President Donald Trump depicting U.S. flag and word "Tariffs" in this illustration taken, April 17, 2025. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration

New: You can now listen to articles.

FAST

SINGAPORE: The Trump administration sticks with its America First trade agenda after a shellacking in the US midterms by firing its latest trade salvo on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan, the European Union and several Southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam.

Singapore could be among the hardest hit despite having a free trade agreement (FTA) and running a trade deficit with the US. Under the proposed duties aimed at what Washington terms as excess industrial capacity, Singapore faces a principal tariff rate of up to 20 per cent from the US.

The latest raft of tariffs, announced on Wednesday (Nov 25) and are not due to kick in until January after a period of consultation, ranged from headline rates of 20 per cent to 40 per cent.

But the US Trade Representative (USTR) has given other governments an out with potential lower rates – if they enter or already have an agreement with the US.

This means those with an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) are not impacted – so long as the agreement remains in force. The European Commission, for instance, said in a statement that it expects any measures imposed by the US to respect the 15 per cent ceiling agreed last year, while rejecting US’ claim that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity.

The proposed tariffs are therefore aimed at pushing those which do not have an ART, such as India, Vietnam and Singapore, to sign one.

Singapore 'very disappointed' with proposed US tariffs, says findings fail to account for its economic structure

Asian governments push back, seek deals after Trump’s new tariff salvo

For example, Vietnam faces a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if it reaches a trade agreement with the US, rising to 35 per cent if negotiations fail. Washington trade insiders expect the Southeast Asian country to sign one on the sidelines of the coming G20 meeting in Miami next month.

India, which remains in talks with the US on a trade deal, would see a 17 per cent tariff rate if an agreement is finalised and a 25 per cent rate if talks fail.

For Singapore, it is 10 per cent with an agreement and 20 per cent without one.

SINGAPORE COULD BE THE HARDEST HIT

Among the 14 trading partners slapped with new tariffs, Singapore stands out as one which has yet to negotiate a trade deal with the US. A 20 per cent rate would also match the Southeast Asian region’s highest rate, presuming Vietnam enters its own ART and similar deals inked by other regional countries remain in force.

“Despite the bilateral FTA and a US trade surplus with Singapore, the Trump administration seems to believe it can extract more and apparently sees little downside risk in trying,” Barbara Weisel of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told me.

Commentary: Trump’s tariff wall isn’t going anywhere

Snap Insight: US midterms – what an angry ‘lame duck’ president could mean for Asia

There may be other reasons for the USTR’s desire to get Singapore to the negotiating table.

At a recent economic conference organised by the American Chamber of Commerce in Singapore, US Ambassador to Singapore Anjani Sinha said that President Donald Trump requires him to “bring some money” back to the US by increasing Singaporean investment.

Singapore’s foreign direct investment in the United States stands at roughly US$72 billion, making it the third largest in Asia, based on the US Department of Commerce’s data as of 2024. Ambassador Sinha said he expects that number to double.

One will expect the US to require Singapore to announce an increase in FDI if a negotiation happens, as it has done with others.

Singapore has previously said it is taking a cautious approach to any concessions that could secure a lower tariff from the US. In a parliamentary reply in August, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said the Singapore government must first assess the significant costs and wider trade implications of measures sought by Washington.

It has also persistently denied that its exports to the world’s largest economy are due to some form of excess capacity.

The country's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry on Thursday morning said it disagrees with the USTR's findings.

WEIGHING THE OPTIONS

Trading partners that do not yet have an ART will have to weigh the actual impact of these potentially higher tariffs versus what they will be required to concede.

Beyond increases in investment commitments, another factor will be what other requirements the US would include, which could relate to trade with China such as those reported to be included in the US negotiations with Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam.

For example, Malaysia agreed to closer cooperation with Washington on export controls, investment screening, transshipment, critical minerals and sensitive technologies – all of which could impact its relations with China. China’s Ministry of Commerce noted last year it had “ serious concerns” regarding parts of the Malaysia-US agreement.

Another ironic twist of these tariffs finds the Trump administration calling foreign governments “unreasonable and unfair” for having their own industrial plans and promoting that their own citizens save money.

An example of the latter is the USTR's mention of Singapore's Central Provident Fund as a policy it deems unreasonable. It had noted that a requirement for citizens to contribute “upwards of 20 per cent of their income” to the programme exceeds that of the US and many developed economies, and that it “promotes savings in a way that depresses consumption”.

In other words, it places tariffs on external governments such as Singapore, for putting their people first.

TARIFFS MAY HAVE A SHORT SHELF-LIFE

The latest trade salvo comes despite US voters making their unhappiness known with the administration’s approach to trade. This should be no surprise though, as Mr Trump's decades-long belief in tariffs will never change.

But the courts have found that the administration often exceeds its authority in issuing them. In February, the US Supreme Court struck down Mr Trump’s so-called “Liberation Day” tariffs. That may again happen here.

The US’ strategy of forcing trading partners to the negotiating table may not work as it once did, given the legal defeats and the likelihood these tariffs may not outlast the administration anyway.

Governments will have to weigh whether to accept a proposed higher rate of tariff under the latest round of “Section 301” probe, which may not last that long, rather than giving up concessions on investment and China-related commitments.

With legal decisions looming and the back half of Trump 2.0 about to start, governments may also reassess how much leverage the US still has.

Steven Okun serves as CEO of APAC Advisors, a geostrategic and responsible investment consultancy based in Singapore. He served as Deputy General Counsel at the US Department of Transportation in the Administration of President Bill Clinton.

It had noted that a requirement for citizens to contribute “upwards of 20 per cent of their income” to the programme exceeds that of the US and many developed economies, and that it “promotes savings in a way that depresses consumption”.
In other words, it places tariffs on external governments such as Singapore, for putting their people first.
TARIFFS MAY HAVE A SHORT SHELF-LIFE

The latest trade salvo comes despite US voters making their unhappiness known with the administration’s approach to trade. This should be no surprise though, as Mr Trump's decades-long belief in tariffs will never change.

But the courts have found that the administration often exceeds its authority in issuing them. In February, the US Supreme Court struck down Mr Trump’s so-called “Liberation Day” tariffs. That may again happen here.
The US’ strategy of forcing trading partners to the negotiating table may not work as it once did, given the legal defeats and the likelihood these tariffs may not outlast the administration anyway.

Governments will have to weigh whether to accept a proposed higher rate of tariff under the latest round of “Section 301” probe, which may not last that long, rather than giving up concessions on investment and China-related commitments.

With legal decisions looming and the back half of Trump 2.0 about to start, governments may also reassess how much leverage the US still has.

items.summary: Jennifer Barreto, 27, has one daughter and two master’s degrees, in research psychology and clinical social work.

New Miss Universe’s Puerto Rican hometown celebrates her historic win as first mother and first married woman to take title

Jennifer Barreto, 27, has one daughter and two master’s degrees, in research psychology and clinical social work.

Puerto Rico's Jennifer Barreto, Miss Universe 2026, attends a press conference after the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico, Wednesday, Nov 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Alejandro Granadillo)

FAST

The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose residents have long been known as “the cucumbers”.

Nestled in the mountains of western Puerto Rico, San Sebastián has been celebrating since Jennifer Barreto made history late Tuesday (Nov 24) as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss Universe.

“It was a day for the history books!” exclaimed one municipal worker at the mayor’s office, which was abuzz with excitement.

The town of some 39,000 people – named after its famous karst formations that look like cucumbers – could barely contain itself.

“La Barreto,” as she’s known, was on the lips of many across San Sebastián hours after the win.

“So excited!” said María Rivera as she juggled orders Wednesday morning at El Guayabal bakery. “We were sure she was going to win.”

Miss Puerto Rico's Jennifer Barreto reacts after winning the Miss Universe at the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico, Tuesday, Nov 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Alejandro Granadillo)

Barreto, 27, has one daughter and two master’s degrees, in research psychology and clinical social work. She also works as a prevention specialist with the US Department of Defense, developing strategies to combat harmful behaviours.

“Her journey is a powerful reminder that motherhood, marriage and personal ambition are not mutually exclusive, and that a woman’s potential should never be defined by the stage of life she is in,” Ronald Day, CEO of the Miss Universe Organization, said in a statement.

The organisation began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023. The pageant has lost favour in some countries, with critics saying it objectifies women and promotes unrealistic body ideals.

Barreto is the sixth Puerto Rican woman to win the Miss Universe crown, ending a 20-year wait for the island.

“I am ready to go to work,” she said at a news conference after the contest, which she called “the Olympics of beauty.”

“You know that I am a highly disciplined woman,” Barreto said, adding that she likes challenges. “I aspire to earn the affection and respect of you all.”

Her hometown became known for “Pepino Power”, a volunteer brigade formed to restore electricity after Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in 2017 as a Category 4 storm.

Puerto Rico now has the third-most Miss Universe titles, behind the United States with nine and Venezuela with seven.

Celebrating Barreto's win was Yazaira Cabrera, a 50-year-old gymnastics coach who loves beauty pageants so much that she had a replica crown made based on the one worn by Puerto Rican Miss Universe 2021 Denise Quiñones.

Cabrera wore it Tuesday night as she watched the contest at home, feeling nervous the entire time.

“They kept us on edge until the very end,” she said. “The whole country was holding its breath.”

Barreto was greeted by thunderous applause at Puerto Rico’s José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum each time she advanced through the competition’s final rounds.

She brought her hands to her face in shock as she was named Miss Universe 2026, beating Miss Dominican Republic and Miss Venezuela. Minutes later, she shimmied in celebration to ABBA’s Dancing Queen.

And thousands of Puerto Ricans across the US territory danced with her.

“It’s a truly spectacular achievement,” San Sebastián Mayor Eladio Cardona Quiles told The Associated Press. “All the most beautiful women in the universe are there, and she managed to stand out. I’m happy she represented ‘los pepinianos.’”

Cardona attended the pageant, while fans gathered in San Sebastián’s public plaza to watch on a big screen. Afterward, they formed a caravan, honking their horns into the night to celebrate Barreto’s victory.

Asian governments push back, seek deals after Trump’s new tariff salvo

Singapore says it is “very disappointed”, Japan calls the proposed duties “regrettable”, while other economies are looking to existing or ongoing trade negotiations to limit the impact.

SINGAPORE: Asian trading partners pushed back against US President Donald Trump’s latest tariff salvo on Thursday (Nov 26), with Singapore saying it was “very disappointed” by the proposed duties and Japan calling the move “regrettable”.

South Korea said it would hold further talks with Washington to safeguard its interests, while Vietnam sought to quickly conclude a trade deal and Taiwan expressed confidence its previously agreed 15 per cent tariff rate would hold.

China and India have also rejected Washington’s claims over excess industrial capacity.

The responses came after the Trump administration proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including some of Asia’s biggest economies and manufacturing hubs.
